rubrics.name: contract_intelligence.v1 — Contract Fidelity Rubric (DRAFT)
rubrics.description: Scores a contract_intelligence.v1 artifact on whether it is a faithful, provenanced, non-inventive carry-through of the client's fetched publishing contract. Every criterion binds to a field that actually exists in the node's output schema (artifact, summary, clientProjectId, clientObjectType, contractSource, bodySchema, idConventions, mediaConvention, mediaPolicy, taxonomy, constraints[], publishPolicy, contract_findings[], assumptions[], blockers[], notes[]). This rubric is the quality half of any cost change to this node: it is designed so that a cheaper or partly deterministic implementation cannot look cheaper-and-equal while quietly softening a client rule.

criteria.name: Contract fidelity — declared rules reproduced, not rewritten
criteria.description: Every rule, field, pattern, literal and constraint the contract declares is reproduced in the output as the contract states it. Structural payloads (bodySchema) are carried whole; rules are carried in the contract's own vocabulary and literals, not paraphrased into cleaner-reading prose, not generalized, not re-ordered into a narrative that loses a clause.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: the pass-through that 'tidies' the contract. A cheaper model summarizing a regex into 'lowercase slug', rounding a byte budget, collapsing two constraints into one, dropping the 'unique across committed legacy posts' half of a uniqueness rule, or re-expressing bodySchema as a bulleted field list instead of the JSON Schema object.

10: bodySchema is present as an actual JSON Schema object with its declared required[] and additionalProperties strictness intact; literal values (id/slug patterns, node id patterns, allowlisted tags, enum members, byte budgets, format preferences, path templates) appear verbatim; every constraint the contract enumerates appears in constraints[] with its own id; idConventions, mediaConvention, taxonomy and publishPolicy each carry the contract's specific text rather than a generic restatement; where mediaPolicy is emitted alongside mediaConvention the two agree exactly (a derived duplicate that contradicts its source is a fidelity defect, not a formatting choice).
7: everything material present, one non-load-bearing clause compressed.
4: a literal is generalized or a pattern is described in words instead of reproduced; or bodySchema is present but reduced below what a downstream node could validate against.
0: bodySchema absent or replaced by prose; a declared constraint missing entirely from constraints[]; a stated limit changed to a different value; or the summary/contract_findings describe a rule in terms that contradict the constraints[] entry it came from.

JUDGING WITHOUT THE SOURCE CONTRACT: score on internal consistency and specificity. Client-specific literals with the shape of a real contract (patterns, path templates, numeric budgets, named registries, named operations) score high; rules stated only as generic prose with no literal, no id and no anchor score low — an output that could have been written without ever reading a contract cannot score above 4 here.

criteria.name: Severity and enforcedLive carried through without downgrade
criteria.description: Each entry in constraints[] carries both the severity the contract assigned and whether it is enforced live, unchanged. A rule the contract declares blocking is never presented as advisory, warning, optional, best-practice or 'should' — in constraints[], in summary, or in contract_findings.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: the single most expensive regression this node can produce — a blocking rule that reaches downstream nodes as advice. Downstream obeys this output, so a downgraded severity ships a rejected or non-compliant object to a live client.

10: every constraints[] entry has an explicit severity AND an explicit enforcedLive value; severity values are drawn from the contract's own vocabulary (e.g. blocks_write / blocks_publish) rather than a substituted scale of the model's own (high/medium/low, error/warning); and the prose in summary, contract_findings and notes describes each blocking rule in blocking language consistent with its entry.
7: all severities and enforcedLive values correct, but one constraint's prose restatement is softer than its declared severity.
4: one or more constraints[] entries omit enforcedLive, or severity is re-expressed in an invented scale that loses the blocks_write/blocks_publish distinction.
0: ANY constraint the contract declared blocking appears as advisory/warning/optional/nice-to-have, OR a blocking constraint is emitted with enforcedLive false, OR severity is absent from an entry so downstream cannot tell blocking from advisory. A single downgrade zeroes this criterion regardless of how many other constraints are correct — there is no partial credit for getting the harmless ones right.

Note for the judge: the node's output schema declares constraints only as a bare array with NO item schema, so severity and enforcedLive are unenforced by validation. This criterion is the only thing checking them.

criteria.name: No invented client rules
criteria.description: Nothing appears in the output that the contract did not declare. Plausible-sounding CMS, SEO or editorial conventions the contract never stated are the exact failure this hunts — they are more dangerous than omissions because they read as authoritative and downstream nodes obey them.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: confident filler. Meta-description length limits, alt-text requirements, heading-hierarchy rules, word counts, canonical-URL conventions, image-dimension advice, publishing cadence, 'best practice' naming — anything that sounds like a CMS and was never in this client's contract. Also hunts invented specifics attached to a real constraint (e.g. asserting a particular object-id convention under a constraint id when the contract only said the id must match its type's pattern).

10: every asserted rule is anchored — it names the constraint id, schema field, registry, policy block or operation it came from; anything not in the contract appears in assumptions[] or notes[] and is explicitly labelled as an assumption or as unmapped, never as a rule.
7: one unanchored but harmless restatement, clearly framed as observation not requirement.
4: an unanchored operational rule stated as though the contract required it, or an assumption promoted into constraints[]/publishPolicy without being marked as an assumption.
0: a concrete requirement appears (a length, a format, a naming rule, a required field, a gate) with no counterpart anywhere in the contract; or assumptions[] is empty while the output nonetheless asserts specifics the contract was silent on. Silence filled confidently is the zero case — the node's own policy is to state silence as an explicit assumption.

JUDGING WITHOUT THE SOURCE CONTRACT: treat anchoring as the proxy. Rules traceable to a named id/field/operation are presumed genuine; free-floating rules that match generic industry convention and carry no anchor are presumed invented.

criteria.name: contractSource provenance — traceable, current, non-placeholder
criteria.description: contractSource identifies the tool the contract came from and when it was fetched, and the asserted rules are traceable to that fetch. Missing or hollow provenance is a hard failure: downstream cannot prove the contract was read rather than remembered.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: the empty-but-valid envelope. The output schema declares contractSource as an object with NO required inner keys, so contractSource {} passes validation cleanly — provenance is only checked here.

5: contractSource names the contract tool actually used and carries a fetchedAtISO timestamp that is a real timestamp from this run (not a rounded, placeholder, obviously-fabricated or far-past value); clientProjectId and clientObjectType are consistent with that source; and where anything was obtained outside the primary fetch (a registry or taxonomy lookup), its own source is identified rather than folded silently into the main contract's provenance.
3: provenance present and plausible but partially specified (tool named, timestamp vague or absent, or a secondary lookup unattributed).
1: contractSource present but generic — no tool name, or a timestamp that is clearly a placeholder.
0: contractSource absent, empty, or asserting a source the rest of the output does not support (e.g. claiming a live fetch while blockers[] or the summary say the contract could not be reached).

VETO: a 0 here fails the whole rubric verdict regardless of aggregate score. An unprovenanced contract is indistinguishable from a remembered one, which is the failure this node exists to prevent.

ENFORCED (Session B2 follow-up, 2026-08-03): a score of 0 here now fails the whole rubric by criticalMin, not by judge instruction — the earlier text asserted this veto but the arithmetic alone (weight 1.5 of 12.5) let a 0 here still score 0.88 and pass. That contradiction is fixed at the mechanism level.

criteria.name: No cross-project or workspace-local conventions
criteria.description: The output describes THIS client only. Rules remembered from another client, from a previously-served brand, or from the workspace's own house schema and habits must not appear. clientProjectId must be the run's registered client, carried from input, never a remembered one.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: identity bleed and habit bleed. This node was branded to a single named client for most of its history and was deliberately generalized; the residue is exactly what regresses first when the node is made cheaper or partly deterministic.

5: clientProjectId matches the client the run is for; clientObjectType is that client's object type; no other client's name, brand, domain, field names, path prefixes, editorial rules or object types appear anywhere in the output, including in notes[], assumptions[] and example text; no workspace-local schema, house field or internal marker is presented as a client requirement; where the contract is silent the output says so rather than borrowing.
3: no wrong-client rule, but a stray reference to another client or to a workspace convention appears in prose without being asserted as a rule.
1: a workspace-local field or internal marker is presented as something the client's contract expects.
0: clientProjectId is a client other than the run's, OR a rule sourced from a different client or from the workspace's own conventions is asserted as this client's requirement. Any single instance is 0 — a rule belonging to someone else is not a partial defect.

criteria.name: Unknown and unmapped contract fields surfaced explicitly
criteria.description: Contract content the node did not recognize or map — including anything the deterministic reduction preserved in its unmapped bucket — is surfaced explicitly as unknown/unmapped rather than dropped silently or guessed at.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: silent loss and silent guessing. The reduction deliberately preserves what it could not classify precisely so this node can hand it forward; dropping it makes the loss invisible to every downstream node and to the operator.

5: unrecognized contract content is present in the output and explicitly labelled as unmapped / not-understood / preserved-for-downstream-attention, with enough of the original content that a downstream node or a human can act on it. Any recognized-but-unused field is likewise noted rather than dropped. Location is flexible — a dedicated unmapped field, notes[], contract_findings[] or assumptions[] all count, since the output schema has no dedicated unmapped field and permits additional properties; what matters is the explicit label.
3: unmapped content is carried but not labelled as unmapped, so downstream cannot tell asserted rules from unclassified residue.
1: only a bare acknowledgement that unmapped content existed, without the content.
0: unmapped or unrecognized content is absent with no acknowledgement (silent drop), OR unrecognized content has been interpreted into a confident rule (guessing) rather than flagged. Both directions are the same failure: the operator loses the signal that something was not understood.

JUDGING WITHOUT THE SOURCE CONTRACT: if the output contains no unmapped/assumption/silence acknowledgement of any kind while asserting a fully-resolved contract, treat that as suspicious rather than perfect — score no higher than 3 unless the output explicitly states that nothing was unmapped.

criteria.name: Blocker honesty — failed or partial fetch is declared, not papered over
criteria.description: When the contract could not be fetched, the client is unreachable, the object type is unsupported, clientProjectId is missing, or the contract declares something the workspace cannot satisfy, the output raises it in blockers[] instead of emitting a confident, complete-looking contract. Conversely, the output does not claim blockers it cannot support.
criteria.guidance:
WHAT THIS HUNTS: the failure mode that manufactures every other failure. When the deterministic prefetch errors, the tempting output is a plausible full contract assembled from memory — which passes schema validation, reads well, and is entirely fabricated. This criterion is the tripwire.

5: the output's confidence matches its evidence. If the contract was fetched, blockers[] is empty and the rules carry provenance. If the fetch failed or was partial, blockers[] names the condition concretely (unreachable client, denied by policy, unsupported object type, missing clientProjectId, unsatisfiable constraint) and the output does NOT go on to assert a full rule set anyway; unfetched areas are absent or marked, not filled.
3: a partial failure is acknowledged in notes[]/assumptions[] but not raised in blockers[], so the conductor does not see it as blocking.
1: a degradation is mentioned only obliquely while the output otherwise presents itself as complete.
0: the output presents a complete, confident contract while its own provenance, summary or notes indicate the fetch failed or was unavailable; or a blocking condition the output itself describes is missing from blockers[]. Inventing a contract over a failed fetch is the maximum-severity case here and should also drive no_invented_client_rules and contract_source_provenance to 0.

metadata.proposedWeightRationale:
HIGHEST WEIGHT, and my recommendation to you: contract_fidelity (3.0) and severity_enforced_live_mapping (2.5) together carry 44% of the rubric. Reason: after the deterministic prefetch landed, this node is no longer a discovery node — it is a validation-and-carry-through step. Almost the only way it can now do damage is by mutating what it was handed, and the most expensive mutation is a blocking rule arriving downstream as advice. Downstream nodes obey this artifact, so a softened severity is a live-client defect, not a style issue. Severity gets its own heavy weight rather than living inside fidelity because the output schema declares constraints as a bare array with no item schema at all — nothing but this rubric checks that severity and enforcedLive survived.

no_invented_client_rules (2.0) is third because invention is the failure mode you named and because it is the one that scales badly: a fabricated rule reads more authoritative than a dropped one and propagates silently through every downstream node.

contract_source_provenance (1.5) and no_cross_project_conventions (1.5) are weighted mid but are written as veto/zero-tolerance criteria in their guidance rather than as sliding scales. Provenance is arithmetically light yet I have marked a 0 there as failing the whole verdict, because contractSource is an object with no required inner keys — an empty contractSource passes schema validation, so a hollow-provenance output would otherwise sail through both the validator and the aggregate. If you would rather see that enforced by arithmetic than by judge instruction, raise its weight to 2.5 and keep the threshold where it is.

unknown_field_surfacing (1.0) and blocker_and_degradation_honesty (1.0) are lightest not because they matter least but because they are closer to binary and rarely partially satisfied; low weight with a hard 0 anchor gets the behaviour without letting either dominate a score.

CORRELATED SCORING IS INTENTIONAL. The criteria are not independent, and the judge is told so: one underlying defect should be scored down on every criterion it violates. A severity downgrade is also a fidelity failure. A contract invented over a failed fetch zeroes invention, provenance and blocker-honesty at once. This is what makes the threshold bite.

PASS THRESHOLD 0.85, chosen against the arithmetic rather than by feel. With these weights and everything else perfect: a 0 on fidelity scores 0.76 (fails), a 0 on severity scores 0.80 (fails), a 0 on invention scores 0.84 (fails). A 0 on provenance alone scores 0.88 and would pass on arithmetic — which is why provenance carries an explicit veto in its guidance. I deliberately did not set the bar at 0.88+, because that would fail an otherwise-clean run for a single soft mark on a light criterion, which would make the rubric noisy exactly when you need it to be a stable comparator across cost trials. 0.85 says: any single top-three collapse fails, and the two zero-tolerance criteria fail by rule.

WHAT THIS BUYS YOU ON COST. This node is $10.87 of $20.95 historical spend and is about to be made partly deterministic. Under this rubric a cheaper or more deterministic implementation can only hold its verdict by reproducing severities, provenance and literals exactly — which is precisely the property determinization should improve, not erode. If a trial comes back cheaper with a held verdict, the saving is real; if the verdict moves, you have the specific criterion that moved and can see whether it was fidelity, severity or invention.
metadata.nodeReadNotes:
READ: the live node record (prompt, input/output schema, allowedTools, modelConfig, 16 version snapshots), the output schema on its own, the assigned contract_intelligence skill, and the most recent real artifact (run_1785435947311_jl8hl4, platform/content_item, 43.7s, ~$0.134). Criteria bind only to fields that exist in that schema.

WHAT THE LIVE NODE CHANGED IN MY DESIGN:

1. It is no longer a discovery node on the normal path. metadata.contractPrefetch is true and the conductor fetches and reduces the contract deterministically in code before the node runs; the node's own prompt calls this "a validation and pass-through step, not a discovery one", with a self-fetch fallback only for old deployments. So the rubric's centre of gravity is carry-through fidelity, not research quality. That is also why partial determinization is a low-risk change IF this rubric holds.

2. The output schema is far weaker than the semantics it carries, and that gap drove three criteria. Only artifact/summary/clientProjectId/clientObjectType/contractSource are required; everything is additionalProperties:true; contractSource is an object with NO required inner keys (so {} validates); and constraints is a bare "array" with NO item schema whatsoever — severity and enforcedLive are completely unenforced by validation. The severity criterion and the provenance criterion are the only checks on those fields anywhere in the system.

3. clientProjectId is the authoritative-identity field added in the W-4 wave specifically because a platform run could otherwise carry another client's identity; the prompt forbids substituting a remembered client. That made cross-project leakage output-judgeable rather than a soft concern — the judge can compare clientProjectId against the run's client directly.

4. The prefetch preserves an "unmapped" bucket, but the output schema has no unmapped field. The real run parked it in notes[] with an explicit "Unmapped contract data preserved for downstream attention" label. So the unknown-field criterion is written to accept any location (notes[], contract_findings[], assumptions[], or an additional property) and to score the explicit LABEL, not the field name — otherwise the rubric would punish the node's actual working convention.

5. mediaPolicy exists in the output schema but is NOT one of the prefetch's declared fields (the prefetch carries mediaConvention). The real output emits both, overlapping. That gave me a concrete, output-only fidelity anchor: a derived duplicate that contradicts its source field is a fidelity defect.

CRITERIA THAT CANNOT BE FULLY JUDGED FROM THE OUTPUT ALONE — stated plainly as you asked:
contract_fidelity, severity_enforced_live_mapping and no_invented_client_rules are strictly comparison criteria. Judging them properly needs the run's prefetchedContract (or the client's live contract) placed beside the output. Ideally the eval harness passes the prefetched contract in as judge context; if it can be, these three become near-deterministic diffs and this rubric gets much sharper. Where the judge has the output only, each of those three carries an explicit "JUDGING WITHOUT THE SOURCE CONTRACT" clause with an internal-consistency proxy: anchoring (does each asserted rule name a constraint id / schema field / operation it came from), specificity (are client-specific literals present, or could this output have been written without reading any contract), and self-consistency (does the prose in summary/contract_findings contradict the severity in constraints[]). Those proxies catch invention and softening reliably; they cannot catch a silent omission of a constraint the judge never saw. That residual blind spot is the honest limit of this rubric and the reason I recommend wiring the prefetched contract into judge context.

DETERMINISTIC MOCK JUDGE: four of the seven have mechanically checkable cores, which should make the plumbing tests meaningful rather than vacuous — contractSource.tool and fetchedAtISO present and non-placeholder; every constraints[] entry having both severity and enforcedLive; clientProjectId equalling the run's projectId; presence of an explicitly-labelled unmapped/assumption entry; blockers[] empty XOR a degradation acknowledged.

EXTRA CRITERION ADDED (one, as permitted): blocker_and_degradation_honesty. Justification — the node's prompt declares an explicit prefetchError path and six named blocker conditions, and nothing in the six required concerns catches the case where the fetch failed and the node emitted a confident, complete-looking, schema-valid contract anyway. That case is how invention actually enters this node in production, and it is fully judgeable from the output (does the artifact's confidence match its own stated evidence). It is deliberately weighted light and written to cascade into the invention and provenance criteria rather than to substitute for them.

NO CRITERIA DROPPED AND NONE MERGED. I considered merging severity into fidelity and rejected it: the schema's total silence on constraint item shape means severity needs its own weight and its own zero anchor, or a downgrade would hide inside a 7/10 fidelity score. I also considered and rejected an envelope-conformance criterion (artifact const, required fields, non-empty summary) — node_validate_output already hard-enforces those, so a rubric criterion there would spend weight on something that cannot fail without the run failing first.

rubrics.name: research_brief.v1 — Evidence Integrity Rubric (draft)
rubrics.description: Scores the `research` node's research_brief.v1 output on whether the evidence it hands to downstream editorial nodes is actually load-bearing: sources proportionate to claim stakes, every substantive claim individually attributed, attributions that hold up, currency appropriate to the topic, real disagreement preserved rather than flattened, explicit claim-risk flags, and coverage of the reader decision the article must serve without silent gaps. Built to be the quality half of cost-optimization comparisons on this node — the failure modes it hunts (dropped browsing, hallucinated or vague attribution, bibliography-instead-of-per-claim sourcing, false consensus) are precisely what a cheaper model or a tighter tool budget erodes first.

criteria.name: Per-Claim Attribution
criteria.description: Each substantive factual claim in the brief carries its own named source at the point the claim is made, rather than the brief presenting assertions alongside a detached source list. Judged over the claim-bearing entries in `notes[]` and any factual assertion in `summary`.
criteria.guidance: 5 = every substantive factual entry names its own source inline (the observed convention is a sourced-fact entry that states the finding and then names the source and, where relevant, its date/version), and any claim that is the agent's own inference is labeled as interpretation rather than dressed as a sourced fact. 3 = most factual entries are individually attributed but several substantive claims float unattributed, or attribution is a bare source name with no indication of which part of it supports the claim. 1 = attribution appears only in a roll-up source-references entry while the body claims are unattributed. 0 = the brief asserts facts with no per-claim attribution anywhere, or the only sourcing is a bibliography sitting next to unsourced assertions. Hunting: the classic degradation where a cheaper run produces confident prose plus a plausible-looking source list that supports none of it in particular. Do NOT award credit for source *volume*; a brief with three claims and three matched sources outscores one with ten claims and twelve unmatched sources. A `summary` that makes a factual claim not traceable to any attributed entry in `notes[]` caps this criterion at 3.

criteria.name: Attribution Integrity (sources say what they are said to say)
criteria.description: Cited sources are represented accurately and within their actual scope — no misattribution, no inflation of a source's authority or specificity, no claim stretched beyond what the cited material supports. Misattribution scores worse than an honest 'unsourced'.
criteria.guidance:
5 = every attribution is specific enough to be checked (named artifact/document/body plus date, version, or identifier), the strength of each claim matches the strength of the cited material, sources are described at their true tier (an internal draft is called an internal draft, not 'the guidance'), and the same source is never invoked to support two claims that contradict each other. 3 = attributions are checkable and broadly fair, but at least one claim is stated more definitively or more specifically than its cited source can carry (e.g. a source describing one product/context is generalized to all). 1 = a source is materially mischaracterized, or a citation is so vague ('studies show', 'industry sources', an unnamed page) that it cannot be checked. 0 = a source is invented, or a cited source is asserted to say something it plainly does not, or a source's stated conclusion is reversed. Hunting: hallucinated and inflated citations — the single most damaging failure for a health-adjacent publisher, because downstream nodes treat this brief as ground truth and will not re-verify. NOTE FOR JUDGE: full verification requires opening the sources, which the output alone does not permit. Judge on what IS visible from the output: attribution specificity, internal consistency between a source's described nature and the weight put on it, claim-vs-source scope match, and any assertion your own knowledge flags as a known misstatement. Score DOWN for unfalsifiable vagueness — a citation that cannot be wrong because it names nothing is a failure of this criterion, not a neutral.

ENFORCED (Session B2 follow-up, 2026-08-03): criticalMin:2 — the rubric author's own recommendation ("treat citation_integrity below 3 as a veto") is now enforced by the harness. Previously a 0 here still scored 0.80 and passed at the old 0.72 threshold; a fluent, confidently-cited, entirely fabricated brief could hold.

criteria.name: Source Authority Proportionate to Stakes
criteria.description: The evidence tier matches what the claim is being asked to bear. For health, medical, safety, regulatory, or financial claims, primary literature, recognized bodies, regulators, and standards outrank vendor pages, content marketing, listicles, and SEO blogs. For product or operational claims, the source-owner's own contract/docs is the authoritative tier.
criteria.guidance: 5 = the highest-stakes claims rest on the highest-authority sources available for that claim type; where only a weaker source exists, the brief says so and marks the claim accordingly rather than letting the weak source pass as authoritative. Correctly ranking its own sources (e.g. treating an owner-published contract as strongest for mechanics while explicitly demoting an internal draft to supporting context) is top-mark behavior. 3 = sources are relevant and non-junk but under-powered for the stakes — secondary summaries or trade press where a primary study or a named body was the appropriate tier — and the gap is not acknowledged. 1 = a medical, safety, or regulatory claim rests primarily on commercial or promotional content, an affiliate/vendor page, or an AI-generated aggregator. 0 = high-stakes claims are supported by sources whose evident purpose is selling the thing being claimed about, with no tier acknowledgement anywhere. Hunting: the authority collapse that happens when a node stops browsing and falls back to whatever is cheapest to recall. Judge tier from what the output names; a brief that names no source type at all cannot earn above 1 here.

criteria.name: Evidence Separation and Claim-Risk Flags
criteria.description: The brief separates sourced fact from interpretation from uncertainty from unsupported assertion, and explicitly flags claims the downstream draft should soften, scope, or drop — with the safer wording or the missing evidence named.
criteria.guidance: 5 = the four epistemic tiers are distinguishable in `notes[]` (sourced facts labeled and attributed, the agent's own synthesis labeled as interpretation, uncertainty stated as such), AND there are specific claim-risk entries that name the tempting-but-unsupported claim and give a safer formulation or state what evidence would be needed. Risk flags are concrete ('do not say X; the evidence supports only Y') rather than generic cautions. 3 = tiers are partially separated and some risk flags exist, but they are generic ('be careful with medical claims') or the interpretation/fact boundary blurs in places. 1 = a single token caution, or risk flags that restate the claims without saying what is wrong with them. 0 = no separation at all — inference, sourced fact, and speculation presented in one undifferentiated confident register, with nothing flagged for softening. Hunting: unsupported certainty on high-stakes claims, which the node's own blocker criteria treat as a stop condition. This is the criterion that most directly protects the draft node from asserting what the research cannot support. JUSTIFICATION FOR INCLUSION: this is the one added criterion; the node's evidence policy makes tier-separation and soften/remove flags a declared deliverable, and none of the six required concerns covers it — 'disagreement surfaced' covers external expert conflict, this covers the brief's own epistemic hygiene about its own claims.

criteria.name: Currency Appropriate to the Topic
criteria.description: Sources are current enough for how fast the topic moves, and their vintage is visible. A superseded guideline, deprecated standard, or stale product behavior presented as current is a failure regardless of how well it is cited.
criteria.guidance: 5 = sourced entries carry a date, version, or fetch timestamp; the brief states currency where the topic is volatile (guidelines, regulation, pricing, product mechanics, anything comparative), and where a source may have been superseded it says so and either verifies or raises it as an open question. 3 = sources are plausibly current and some dating is present, but vintage is inconsistent or the brief never addresses whether a fast-moving claim is still true. 1 = no dating or versioning anywhere, leaving currency unassessable, on a topic where currency clearly matters. 0 = a superseded guideline, withdrawn recommendation, retracted study, or deprecated behavior is presented as current fact. Hunting: the specific damage of a run that skipped its browsing budget and answered from stale memory. Note that undated is not automatically stale — but on a source-sensitive claim, undated is not better than 1, because a downstream editor cannot tell. Age alone is not a penalty where the source is a settled primary reference; penalize age only where the topic has moved.

criteria.name: Genuine Disagreement and Uncertainty Preserved
criteria.description: Where credible expert opinion actually diverges, or where evidence is thin, contested, or mixed, the brief states the divergence and who holds which position — instead of collapsing it into a single confident consensus line for the draft to repeat.
criteria.guidance: 5 = real disagreements are named with the sides identified and, where possible, the reason for the split (different populations, different endpoints, older versus newer evidence, or an unresolved question), and thin-evidence areas are called thin. Open questions are specific and answerable, not filler. 3 = the brief acknowledges some uncertainty but in general terms, without naming who disagrees or what the competing positions are. 1 = a single hedging sentence stands in for a genuinely contested field. 0 = a contested question is presented as settled consensus, or the brief manufactures a clean answer where the evidence does not have one. Hunting: false consensus — the most invisible failure, because a flattened brief reads better than an honest one and downstream nodes will confidently publish it. Manufactured balance is also penalized: inventing a 'controversy' where the evidence is genuinely one-sided scores no better than 2, because it misleads the draft as surely as flattening does.

criteria.name: Coverage of the Downstream Decision, Gaps Declared
criteria.description: The brief actually covers what the brief/draft nodes need to write the article — the reader decision it must serve, the material claims, practical implications, and constraints — and any area it could not cover is stated as an explicit gap or blocker rather than silently omitted.
criteria.guidance: 5 = `artifact` is exactly the declared artifact constant, `summary` states the evidence position in a way a downstream node can act on, and `notes[]` covers the reader's actual decision with practical implications, not just abstract facts; every area the research could not settle appears as a named open question or blocker. Declared gaps are a strength here, not a deduction. 3 = the substantive ground is covered but implications are thin (facts with no 'so what for the reader'), or coverage is uneven with an unacknowledged soft spot. 1 = the brief covers a topic adjacent to the reader decision rather than the decision itself, or is padded to length with restatements of the input. 0 = the artifact constant is wrong or missing, `summary` is empty//placeholder, or the brief silently omits a material area the article cannot be written without — silent gaps score 0 here even when what IS present is good, because a downstream node cannot detect them. NOTE FOR JUDGE: fully assessing coverage requires the node's declared required input (the reader-insight dependency). Where that input is available to you, judge coverage against the reader decision it names. Where it is not, judge the judgeable proxy: internal completeness, whether implications are drawn for a reader at all, and whether limits are declared explicitly — and do not infer coverage from length.

Highest weight goes to ATTRIBUTION INTEGRITY (2.0) and PER-CLAIM ATTRIBUTION (1.8) — together 40% of the normalized total. Reasoning: this node is upstream of every editorial node, and downstream nodes treat its output as ground truth without re-verifying. A misattributed or unsupported claim here does not get caught later; it gets published under a client's name. For a health-adjacent client that is the failure with real-world consequences, so misattribution is weighted above every other concern, and I wrote the guidance so that vague-but-unfalsifiable citation scores DOWN rather than neutral — otherwise the cheapest way to score well is to cite nothing checkable.

These two are also the most cost-sensitive criteria in the set, which matters because this rubric's job is to be the quality half of cost comparisons. When a model is downgraded or the tool budget tightened on this node, the first things to go are real fetches and specific attributions — the prose stays fluent while the evidence hollows out. A rubric that weighted "brief coverage" or readability highest would score a hollowed-out brief as unchanged and certify an unmeasured downgrade as a win. Source authority (1.5) is weighted third for the same reason: it degrades silently and is judgeable from the output.

Claim-risk flagging (1.3) is my one added criterion and I put it above recency and disagreement because the node's own evidence policy makes tier-separation and soften/remove flags a declared deliverable, and it is the mechanism that protects the draft node from over-claiming. Recency (1.2) and brief coverage (1.2) sit in the middle. Disagreement surfaced (1.0) is lowest not because it is unimportant but because it is the most topic-contingent — many briefs cover subjects with no genuine expert split, and a high weight there would penalize honest briefs on settled topics. Its guidance penalizes manufactured balance for exactly that reason.

passThreshold 0.72: with scaleMax 5 uniform across criteria, this is roughly a weighted average of 3.6/5. That is deliberately above "meets the contract with visible soft spots" (3.0) and below "clean" (4.0+). A brief that is well-sourced on most claims but has one stretched attribution and thin implications lands near 3.4 and fails — which is what I want, because at a health publisher that brief is not safe to build on. A brief that is honestly sourced, dated, tier-separated, and declares its gaps lands 4.0+ and passes even if it is short. Two operator decisions I recommend on top of the aggregate, which the schema cannot express: (1) treat citation_integrity below 3 as a veto regardless of total — a brief with an invented or reversed citation should never pass on the strength of its other criteria; (2) when using this rubric for cost-reduction comparisons, require the per-criterion scores on citation_integrity and per_claim_support to be held or improved, not just the aggregate, since a cheaper run can trade evidence quality for coverage breadth and hold the total flat.
metadata.nodeReadNotes:
Read the live node record (prompt, input/output schema, allowed tools, model limits, revision history) and one real research_brief.v1 artifact from the most recent run, to bind criteria to fields that exist.

What the live node revealed that shaped the criteria:

1. THE OUTPUT SCHEMA IS ALMOST EMPTY. It requires only the artifact constant and a non-empty summary string, with an optional array of note strings and additionalProperties open. Nothing about sources, claims, or risk is schema-enforced. So the real contract lives in the node's prompt, which declares five payload categories the brief must produce — sourced facts, practical implications, claim-risk notes, open questions, and source references — plus an evidence policy requiring separation of sourced fact / interpretation / uncertainty / unsupported claim and flagging of claims to soften or remove. I bound the criteria to those declared obligations rather than to the thin schema, and folded artifact-constant and summary-presence checks into brief_coverage as a 0-anchor so the schema-level contract is still scored somewhere.

2. THE REAL ARTIFACT USES A LABELED-NOTE CONVENTION that the schema does not require: entries prefixed as sourced fact (with source and date, and often a practical implication attached), interpretation, claim risk, open question, and a closing source-references roll-up. Because this convention is emergent rather than enforced, I described it in guidance as "the observed convention" and scored the underlying property (per-claim attribution, tier separation) rather than the literal prefix strings — otherwise the rubric would reward string-matching and would break the moment the prompt is reworded.

3. THE NODE DOES NOT BROWSE BY DEFAULT. Its cost policy restricts web search/fetch to claims that are current, comparative, regulatory, or otherwise source-sensitive, and it pushes stricter evidence bars down to the client record (a recent revision stripped the hardcoded medical client out of the prompt). Two consequences: source_authority and recency guidance are written to judge tier and currency *proportionate to the claim's stakes* rather than demanding external sources unconditionally; and the observed artifact legitimately cites internal/owner artifacts rather than URLs, so citation_integrity is written to score attribution specificity and tier honesty, not URL presence.

CRITERIA THAT CANNOT BE FULLY JUDGED FROM THE OUTPUT ALONE — stated plainly:

- CITATION ACCURACY is the important one. Verifying that a source says what it is said to say requires opening the source, which the output does not permit and which a mock judge certainly cannot do. My judgeable proxies, written into the criterion's guidance: attribution specificity (named artifact/body plus date or version), claim-vs-source scope match (is the claim stated more broadly than the cited material can carry), source-tier honesty (is an internal draft called an internal draft), internal consistency (same source invoked for contradictory claims), and anything the judge's own knowledge flags as a known misstatement. Critically, I made unfalsifiable vagueness score DOWN rather than neutral, because otherwise the proxy is trivially gamed by citing nothing checkable. The operator should know this criterion is a proxy and that a spot-check of actual sources on a sample of runs is still required — the rubric narrows the gap, it does not close it.

- BRIEF COVERAGE cannot be fully judged without the node's declared required input (its reader-insight dependency), which names the reader decision the article must serve. Where the judge has that input contract, coverage should be scored against it; where it does not, the guidance directs judging internal completeness, whether reader-facing implications are drawn at all, and whether limits are declared — with an explicit instruction not to infer coverage from length. Silent gaps are by definition undetectable from the output; the best available lever is to reward explicitly declared gaps, which I did (declared gaps are a strength, not a deduction), so that honest incompleteness outscores confident incompleteness.

- RECENCY is partly proxied. The judge can see dates and versions where present and can catch known-superseded guidance from its own knowledge, but cannot confirm that an undated source is current. Guidance therefore caps undated source-sensitive claims rather than assuming staleness, and penalizes age only where the topic actually moves.

ADDED CRITERION AND WHY: I added exactly one — claim_risk_flagging (evidence separation plus soften/remove flags). It is not a duplicate of disagreement_surfaced: that criterion covers *external* expert divergence, this covers the brief's *own* epistemic hygiene about its *own* claims, which the node's prompt makes a first-class deliverable and which its blocker criteria treat as a stop condition (unsupported certainty on high-stakes claims). No listed concern was dropped and none were merged.

One operational note for the operator, outside the rubric: the last recorded run of this node completed in ~49s and the run failed downstream on budget exhaustion at other nodes. If this rubric is used for cost trials, the research node's own budget is not where the run is currently breaking — which makes it a poor first candidate for cost reduction and a good candidate for holding steady as a quality baseline.

Left below the 0.85 used by the more mechanically-checkable rubrics on purpose: several of this rubric's criteria are proxies by the original author's own admission (citation accuracy needs the source opened, which no judge here can do), and pretending otherwise would make the bar noisy rather than honest.

rubrics.name: article_body — client object build quality (DRAFT v1)
rubrics.description: Scores one client_object.v1 envelope emitted by the article_body builder: whether the body is shaped to the client's own fetched contract, whether contract-declared private annotations are actually populated on every node, whether media references are safe and current-request, whether client validation is reported honestly, whether the piece reads as one deliberate article grounded in the approved upstream editorial decisions, and whether missing inputs produce explicit blockers instead of invented values. Designed as the quality half of cost-optimization comparisons: a cheaper model must hold or improve this verdict.

criteria.name: Client-schema compliance of body
criteria.description: body is shaped to the client's own declared contract: the contract's root field names and nesting, opaque node ids matching the contract's id pattern, no undeclared/workspace-only keys when the contract is strict, and every enum-valued field carrying a value drawn from the contract's own declared enum rather than an invented, pluralized, or approximated one.
criteria.guidance:
SEAM RULE (Wolf, 2026-08-03): a field crosses into the client object iff the client's contract declares it, and its CONTENT belongs to the publication, not to the CMS agent's own profession. CMS-agent-owned material — general writing craft, DTC/marketing technique, security notes, run limitations, AI operating conditions, workflow commentary — must never appear inside body regardless of what the field is named. Publication-owned material — this piece's subject, this client's rules, this object's structure — may appear only where the contract declares it. A field name blacklist is the wrong test (a workspace habit dressed up as a name check); judge the CONTENT of each field against this rule instead.

10: every field in body is either explicitly anchored to the contract (named in notes/contractSource as contract-declared) or is plainly publication-specific content about THIS piece — no field carries general craft guidance, an AI run condition, a security/limitation note, or workflow-process commentary; node ids are opaque and pattern-consistent (e.g. n_a1, n_b2 — never slug/topic/intent-revealing); every enum-shaped value is a single lowercase token repeated consistently, stated as coming from the contract's own enum.
7: shape is clearly client-derived but one enum-shaped field carries a value used only once and unexplained, or ids are pattern-valid but semantically revealing.
4: body is client-shaped in the main but contains one field whose content is CMS-agent's own craft/process material rather than publication content, or one enum value is a near-miss of a sibling value elsewhere.
0: body carries CMS-agent's own professional or process material (general writing craft advice, an AI run limitation, a security caveat, workflow/pipeline commentary) inside a client-facing field; OR a field has no contract anchor and its content is not plainly this-publication-specific; OR body is a generic workspace article shape (title/sections/paragraphs) rather than the client's object; OR ids encode topic/intent; OR enum fields carry free-text prose. Do NOT award credit for richness — more fields is worse, not better, if the contract is strict. The judge cannot see the contract itself unless it is supplied as evidence; absent that, score internal consistency, self-declared provenance of enum values, and whether each field's CONTENT reads as profession-material or publication-material, and say which basis was used.

criteria.name: Private annotations populated on every node
criteria.description: The contract-declared per-node private annotation fields (e.g. private.strategy, private.intent, plus the contract's free-text notes field) are actually present and non-empty on EVERY emitted node, with enum values from the contract's own enums and a one-sentence reason in the notes field. This is a known live gap — an entire historical run emitted every node with private absent.
criteria.guidance: This criterion is counted, not impressed. Count N = number of emitted nodes in body; count P = nodes carrying a non-empty private block with BOTH a non-empty strategy-equivalent AND a non-empty intent-equivalent. 5: P == N, every value is a single token from a consistent closed set, and the contract's free-text private notes field carries a specific one-sentence reason for THAT node (not a restatement of the node's own title); OR the output states, in notes, that the contract declares no private annotation fields for this object type and adds none. 4: P == N and enums are clean but two or more notes strings are generic filler reused across nodes. 3: P >= 0.8N. 2: P >= 0.5N. 1: private appears on at least one node. 0: private is absent, empty, or null on every node — this is the known live failure and must score 0 even if the article is otherwise excellent; also 0 if the node silently omits private and does not state that the contract declares none. Empty strings, nulls, and 'n/a' count as absent. A private block that exists but whose strategy/intent are prose sentences rather than enum tokens caps this criterion at 2.

criteria.name: Media reference safety and presence
criteria.description: Every media reference in body is a verified current-request artifact expressed in the form the contract demands for that field (rendered fields get the client's public serving path, raw reference fields get the artifact key), and artifactReferences plus mediaPathConvention corroborate it. Pattern validity is not proof of provenance. As of Wolf's 2026-08-05 ruling, images are a DEFAULT REQUIREMENT for most articles — a text-only piece must earn that as a stated, specific exception, not merely note that nothing upstream requested media.
criteria.guidance:
POLICY (Wolf, 2026-08-05): images are required for most articles; exceptions should be few. A no-media body is not neutral by default — it must justify itself as one of the genuine exceptions (e.g. a short reference/glossary entry, a pure text update to an already-published object, or the client's own contract signaling this object type carries no media) to hold full marks. 'Nothing upstream called for it' is necessary but not by itself sufficient.

5: either (a) body includes media, and every reference in it resolves to an entry in artifactReferences that names this request/run and records that the artifact tool verified it, in the correct form for its field (rendered fields get the client's public serving path, raw reference fields get the artifact key), with any contract-required placement/rendering metadata present; or (b) body has no media AND the output names a SPECIFIC, legitimate reason this particular piece is a genuine exception under the policy above — not just that the upstream artifact_plan/input didn't request one, but why this piece in particular doesn't need one.
3: body has no media and the output states only that none was called for upstream, with no specific exception reason for this piece — under the new default this is a real, if moderate, defect, not a clean pass. Also 3 if media is present, correctly formed and listed in artifactReferences, but the output offers no evidence the artifact was verified for THIS request (bare key, no verification/run marker).
1: a reference is well-formed against the stated pattern but artifactReferences is empty or does not cover it — pattern validity claimed as proof.
0: any of the following appears anywhere in body: an http:// or https:// remote media URL, a data: URI, a repository or filesystem path (src/, /assets/, ./, ../, *.png relative path), a hand-authored or placeholder key, a reference bearing another slug's or another request's identifier, or a raw artifact key placed in a field the output itself describes as rendered. A single instance of any of these is 0 regardless of how many other references are clean. Also 0 if the body omits a media slot that the approved artifact_plan called for, with no note or blocker explaining the omission — a cost-motivated drop dressed as a clean text-only piece. The judge cannot confirm materialization with the artifact tool; score the corroboration the output carries and note that limit.

criteria.name: Grounding in approved upstream editorial output
criteria.description: The body executes the approved review/aggregation decisions and the chosen angle and narrative arc, rather than re-litigating them, silently dropping required elements, or substituting a fresh editorial plan of the node's own.
criteria.guidance: 10: the body visibly delivers the elements the output itself attributes to upstream (the angle/promise, the arc's movement and resolution, and named build instructions such as a requested example, table, or checklist), each such element is actually present in body, and any departure is recorded in assumptions with a reason. Private notes that map each node to its role in the arc are strong evidence. 7: all attributed elements are present but one is executed thinly (named but not developed). 4: the body is competent yet at least one element the output claims came from upstream is missing from body, or the summary/notes describe a different structure than the body delivers. 2: the output argues with the upstream decision — reopening the angle, second-guessing the approved scope, or editorializing about what review should have said. 0: no traceable relationship between the stated upstream inputs and what body contains; the node evidently wrote its own brief. Contradiction between the envelope's own prose (summary, notes, assumptions) and body content is the strongest available negative signal — use it. The judge does not receive the upstream node outputs; grounding is scored on internal traceability and self-consistency only.

criteria.name: Editorial coherence as one deliberate piece
criteria.description: The reader-visible copy reads as a single article with one voice, one through-line, and real transitions — not as independently generated sections stapled together.
criteria.guidance: 10: the opening sets a tension the closing resolves; sections advance an argument in an order that could not be shuffled without loss; each section hands off to the next; terminology, person, and tense are stable throughout; summary/checklist nodes restate the piece's own claims rather than introducing new ones. 7: coherent and well-ordered but one or two sections could be reordered freely, or one transition is missing. 4: sections are individually fine but interchangeable — each restates the premise from scratch, or the same definition is re-explained in three places. 2: visible register or voice shifts between sections, or the closing does not answer the opening. 0: fragments with no through-line, contradictory claims between sections, template scaffolding left in the copy ('In this section we will...', 'Section 3:', lorem/TODO/placeholder text), or a body whose nodes are clearly separate answers to separate prompts. Length, section count, and formatting richness earn nothing here.

criteria.name: Honest client-validation status
criteria.description: clientValidation truthfully reports the CLIENT's own validator result — the tool used, whether it was reached, the verdict, and the client's own issue text — including when the verdict is failure or a deferral because the object does not yet exist.
criteria.guidance: 5: clientValidation names the client tool actually called, records attempted true/false, a boolean valid, and issues quoting the client's own refusal text; failure and the 'requires_existing_object' deferral are reported plainly as what they are, with valid left false; if the validator could not be reached at all, attempted is false AND a blocker is present. 3: verdict is reported but thin — no issues text, or the tool is unnamed, so the claim cannot be traced to the client. 1: clientValidation is present but self-graded — the node asserts validity without naming a client call, or reports a workspace/self check as if it were the client's verdict. 0: clientValidation is absent entirely, or claims valid true while blockers/issues elsewhere in the output contradict it, or reports the node as blocked because the approval-gated write tool was unavailable (the read-only validator surface needs no approval — citing that as a block is a false report). Reporting a deferral or an outright failure honestly must score at or above 4; do not penalize an honest 'not valid'.

criteria.name: Explicit blockers instead of invented data
criteria.description: When a contract-required field, a taxonomy term, a media artifact, a client identity, a link, or a fact is missing, the node blocks and names the gap in blockers/assumptions rather than emitting a plausible-looking invented value.
criteria.guidance: 5: every gap is surfaced — blockers name the specific unsatisfiable requirement in terms a human can act on, assumptions record each judgement call and why, and the body visibly declines to fabricate (e.g. CTA text with no link because no approved URL was supplied; taxonomy omitted and stated, rather than guessed). 3: gaps are surfaced but described vaguely ('some fields incomplete') so the operator cannot act. 2: the output is silent about a gap that its own body reveals (a field left empty with no note). 0: an invented value is present and passed off as real — a fabricated URL, DOI, statistic, citation, date, author, taxonomy term, product name, or artifact key; or the node reports itself unblocked while a contract-required field is unsatisfied. A confident, well-formed value with no provenance is the exact failure this criterion hunts: prefer an explicit blocker over a plausible fill every time. Do not reward long blocker lists as such — reward specificity and their agreement with the body.

criteria.name: No workflow language in reader-visible text
criteria.description: Reader-visible strings carry no pipeline, agent, prompt, scoring, or internal-process vocabulary; internal reasoning lives only in the contract's designated private/internal fields.
criteria.guidance: Scan only reader-visible fields (titles, decks, descriptions, body prose, labels, list items, CTA text, SEO fields, slug and ids). 5: none of the following appears in any reader-visible string: node, node id, prompt, agent, workflow, pipeline, conductor, stage, upstream/downstream, artifact key, schema, enum, blocker, assumption, rubric, score, token, model name, tool name, run id, or internal role names such as review_aggregator / angle_strategy. Domain terms that the ARTICLE is legitimately about (e.g. an article about publishing operations using the word 'publish' or 'validation' as its subject matter) are not violations. 3: one borderline leak — an internal-sounding label or a bracketed aside. 1: a private note, strategy label, or instruction fragment appears verbatim in a reader-visible field. 0: reader-visible text addresses the pipeline or the operator-of-the-agent rather than the reader, ids encode strategy or intent, or internal annotation is emitted into a public field. Judge the strings as a reader would encounter them; do not penalize the envelope's own summary/notes/assumptions, which are internal by design.

criteria.name: Envelope provenance and contract sourcing
criteria.description: The output envelope is exactly the node's declared shape and carries real contract provenance: artifact equals the schema's required constant, contractSource records how and when the client contract was fetched, and clientProjectId/clientObjectType are carried through unchanged and consistently with contractSource and with the body's own shape.
criteria.guidance: 5: artifact is exactly the schema's declared constant 'client_object.v1'; summary is a real one-paragraph account of what was built and what happened to validation; contractSource names the client tool the contract came from and when it was fetched; clientProjectId and clientObjectType are non-empty, agree with contractSource and with the object the body evidently is; the JSON is the envelope itself, not wrapped in output/data/result/actual or fenced markdown. 3: all required fields present but contractSource is a bare or contentless object (no tool, no timestamp) — provenance asserted rather than shown. 1: artifact carries a stale or wrong constant (e.g. the retired 'article_body.v1'), or summary is a one-line restatement of the title. 0: a required envelope field is missing or empty; or the object is wrapped in a container key or prose; or contractSource is absent, meaning nothing establishes that a client contract was fetched at all — the node's own blocker criteria make missing contract provenance a stop condition, so an envelope without it is a build that should never have completed.
