metadata.proposedWeightRationale:
Highest weight goes to CLIENT-SCHEMA COMPLIANCE (3.0). This node is the only place the client's own object shape is constructed, and the node's own canonical rules say the fetched contract is the sole authority; a body in the wrong shape is unpublishable no matter how well written, and it is also the failure a cheaper model is most likely to introduce (drifting back to a generic article shape it has seen a thousand times).

Joint second: PRIVATE ANNOTATIONS (2.75) and MEDIA SAFETY (2.75). Private annotations are weighted deliberately high because you asked the known live gap to be visible, and because it is countable — P out of N nodes — so it is the cleanest non-gameable signal in the rubric. Media safety is weighted equally because it is the only criterion where a single instance is an unrecoverable publish defect (a repo path or a copied key from another request can put the wrong image on a client's live page), and because "pattern-valid key" is exactly the kind of plausible-looking output a cheaper model produces confidently.

Middle: GROUNDING (1.75) and EDITORIAL COHERENCE (1.75) — these are what the reader and the client actually pay for, but they are also the most judge-subjective, so I kept them below the mechanical criteria on purpose. If cost-optimization comparisons start turning on judge noise, these two are where it will come from.

Lower: EXPLICIT BLOCKERS (1.5) and HONEST VALIDATION (1.5) — both are integrity criteria and both matter enormously, but the downstream publish gate re-validates and a human reads blockers, so a lapse here is caught rather than shipped. ENVELOPE PROVENANCE (1.25) is my one added criterion; it is mostly mechanical, but I found the live stored output emits artifact "article_body.v1" while the schema now requires the constant "client_object.v1", so this is currently a real, silent, live defect that no other criterion catches. NO WORKFLOW LANGUAGE (1.0) is lowest not because leakage is acceptable but because it is rare, cheap to detect, and rarely the thing that separates two model configurations.

passThreshold 0.85, chosen against the arithmetic rather than by feel. Total weight is 17.25. With that spread, a total failure (score 0) on any single one of the three heaviest criteria drops a run below the bar even if every other criterion is flawless: schema-0 caps at 0.826, private-0 at 0.841, media-0 at 0.841 — all fail. That is the intended property: the known private-annotation gap alone must fail a run, not merely dent it. A zero on grounding alone caps at 0.899 and would still pass, which I accept — grounding failures do not occur in isolation and will drag coherence and schema with them. Guidance is anchored so that "no defect found" earns full marks rather than "exceptional", which keeps 0.85 reachable by a correct run instead of turning it into a beauty contest. If you want media to also be a standalone hard gate with margin rather than by two points, raise its weight to 3.0; if 0.85 proves too tight in practice, lower the threshold before flattening the weights — the weight shape is the opinion, the threshold is the dial.
metadata.nodeReadNotes:
Read the live node record (prompt, schema, outputSchema, allowedTools, modelConfig, 18 revisions) and the most recent stored output (artifact_article_body_1785437050279, run_1785435947311_jl8hl4).

What the live node shaped: the output envelope is deliberately thin — artifact (const), summary, clientProjectId, clientObjectType, contractSource, body (free-form object), plus optional clientValidation, artifactReferences, mediaPathConvention, assumptions, blockers, notes. Every criterion above binds to one of those fields; I added none that reference fields the schema does not have. The prompt's own blocker list (no contract provenance, clientProjectId disagreement, unsatisfiable required fields, unresolved taxonomy, unverified media) is what the blockers and provenance criteria are calibrated against, and its client-validation policy explicitly makes the "requires_existing_object" deferral a NORMAL outcome — so the honesty criterion scores an honest deferral at full marks rather than treating it as failure. The node is write-prohibited and reaches the client only through the read-only surface; reporting itself blocked because the approval-gated write tool was unavailable is a false report, which is why that specific move is a 0 anchor.

Limits — criteria that cannot be judged from the output alone, with the proxy I used:
1. The client contract is NOT carried in the output. contractSource records only how it was fetched (in the live sample: {tool: object_contract, fetchedAtISO}). A judge therefore cannot verify required-field coverage, additionalProperties:false, id patterns, or enum membership against the real contract. Proxy in client_schema_compliance and private_annotations: internal consistency of enum-shaped values across nodes, self-declared provenance of those enums in notes, and detection of workspace tells. Stated inside the guidance so the judge does not overclaim.
2. Upstream outputs (review_aggregator, contract_intelligence, narrative_movement, angle_strategy) are not in this node's output. Grounding is scored on internal traceability — whether elements the envelope itself attributes to upstream actually appear in body, and whether summary/notes/assumptions agree with body. Contradiction between the envelope's prose and its body is the strongest available negative signal.
3. Artifact materialization cannot be confirmed; the judge cannot call the artifact tool. Media safety scores the corroboration carried in artifactReferences/mediaPathConvention and hard-fails the forms that are self-evidently wrong (remote URL, data URI, repo path, foreign-slug reference).

My one added criterion, envelope_provenance_integrity, is justified by something the live read revealed: at workspace v260 the schema's artifact constant was renamed to client_object.v1 and produces was updated, but the latest stored output still emits artifact "article_body.v1", and the execution record still lists produces ["article_body.v1"]. None of the eight required concerns catches a stale envelope constant or an empty contractSource, and missing contract provenance is a declared stop condition in the node's own prompt — so an envelope that completes without it is a build that should not exist. It also catches the prompt's explicit "do not wrap in actual/output/data/result/markdown" rule.

One honest correction to the brief's premise: the run I read (jl8hl4, 13 emitted nodes) DOES populate private.strategy/private.intent/agentNotes on every node, with values from a consistent closed set. The all-empty-private failure you cited belongs to the earlier run 9u5mjz, which is what drove workspace revisions v237/v238 (adding narrative_movement and angle_strategy as dependencies and the private-annotation policy). So the gap appears to have been addressed since — which makes it exactly the kind of thing a cost reduction could silently regress, and is a further reason to weight it as heavily as I have. The criterion is written as a count so a regression shows up as a number, not an impression.
metadata.sessionB2FollowupRevision: client_schema_compliance rewritten from a field-name blacklist to Wolf's seam test (profession-content never crosses regardless of field name; publication-content crosses only if contract-declared). media_safety's full-marks branch for 'no media present' now requires that no media was actually called for, closing the loophole where dropping images held a clean score while saving artifact_plan's cost.

rubrics.name: publish_payload — dry-run publish candidate integrity (DRAFT)
rubrics.description: Scores a single `dry_run_publish_payload.v1` output from the publishing_conductor `publish_payload` node. This node is an adapter: it assembles the client-shaped publish candidate from the approved `article_body` output plus `artifact_plan`, and it must build without publishing. The rubric is deliberately a conformance rubric, not a quality rubric — every criterion binds to a declared field of the node's output schema (artifact, dryRun, clientProjectId, clientObjectType, contractSource, clientObject, requestId, clientValidation, artifactProtocol, artifactReferences, artifactHandling.legacyFallbacksUsed, validationAssumptions, blockers, notes) or to a declared policy in the node prompt. It is the quality half of any future cost reduction on this node: a cheaper model that still holds these scores is an optimization; one that drops them is a downgrade.

criteria.name: Publish gates preserved and honestly reported
criteria.description: The payload keeps every approval/readiness gate intact: dryRun is literally true, artifact is exactly the declared artifact id, the client's own validator verdict is reported as it actually came back, and blockers are stated explicitly rather than softened, deferred to prose, or pre-satisfied.
criteria.guidance: Full marks (5): `dryRun` is boolean true and `artifact` is exactly "dry_run_publish_payload.v1"; `clientValidation` records the real verdict from the CLIENT's own read-only validator (tool + operation + valid + issues, each issue keeping the severity the client returned); if validation could not be obtained, clientValidation.attempted is false AND a corresponding blocker exists; every unmet condition named anywhere in the output (unverified media, missing draft record, unresolved review, unreachable client) also appears as a string in `blockers`; the summary's readiness claim matches `blockers` rather than overstating it. Score 3: gates are technically present but one is weakened — e.g. a client-returned "error" or "blocker" issue is restated at a lower severity, or a real obstacle appears only in `notes`/`validationAssumptions` instead of `blockers`. Score 0 — any of: `dryRun` absent, false, or the string "true"; `clientValidation.valid` asserted true without a client tool call recorded, or inherited from an upstream/workspace verdict, or a workspace-local schema check presented as the client's verdict; the node reports itself blocked *by* the approval-gated project.call_tool instead of using project.call_read_tool (a fabricated excuse for skipping the gate); `blockers` empty while the body of the output describes unresolved conditions; or the payload is framed as approved/ready-to-publish. The operator opened publishing globally on 2026-07-31, so a payload that flatters its own readiness is the failure this criterion exists to catch — err toward 0 whenever honesty and convenience point in different directions.

criteria.name: Exact mapping from the approved article_body
criteria.description: clientObject is a faithful transformation of the client-shaped body approved upstream by article_body — a shape/field mapping only. Content added, rewritten, trimmed, reordered, or paraphrased at this node is a failure regardless of whether it reads better.
criteria.guidance:
Judge against the upstream article_body output when it is supplied alongside this output; otherwise use the proxies below. Full marks (5): every content-bearing value in `clientObject` (title, slug, deck/description, seo fields, node bodies, source URLs, claim texts, CTA text) is traceable to the approved body verbatim; differences are confined to structural placement demanded by the client contract; `notes`/`validationAssumptions` state plainly what was carried through and what, if anything, was intentionally omitted and why (e.g. taxonomy omitted because terms do not resolve). Score 3: mapping is substantially faithful but one non-trivial value is silently altered — a retitled heading, a tightened meta description, a dropped source entry — with no note declaring it. Score 0 — any of: prose in `clientObject` that was authored at this node rather than carried from the approved body; a source URL, statistic, claim, or CTA destination that appears here and not upstream (fabricated evidence is the worst case); approved sections dropped without a declared blocker or note; or the summary claims fidelity while the object visibly diverges. Absence of an upstream body to diff against is not a reason to award full marks — an output that gives the judge no traceable basis for fidelity (no notes on what was carried, unexplained new content) caps at 2.

RECONCILED WITH no_workspace_fields (Session B2 follow-up, 2026-08-03): these two criteria previously contradicted each other on fields like publication_context — no_workspace_fields scored their presence as an automatic 0, while this criterion scored their omission as an automatic 0, so no output could satisfy both. Resolved by the seam: content that no_workspace_fields correctly strips (CMS-agent's own professional/process material) is NOT a fidelity violation to omit here — omitting it is required, not a deviation, and must not be penalized. A real fidelity violation is dropping or altering PUBLICATION-specific content the contract declares should carry through unchanged.

criteria.name: Artifact keys vs public serving paths, correctly placed and correctly severed
criteria.description: Every media reference sits in the form its target field demands — public serving path in rendered fields, raw artifact key only in the contract's designated reference fields — carries current-request verification evidence, and artifactProtocol/artifactHandling report the client's protocol truthfully.
criteria.guidance: Full marks (5): `artifactProtocol` names the protocol as the client's own contract names it (not workspace jargon) and states the raw-key vs public-path forms; every entry in `artifactReferences` carries verification evidence that the reference was materialized by that protocol for the CURRENT request; rendered fields inside `clientObject` hold resolved public paths, raw keys appear only in the contract's designated reference fields; document artifacts are delivered as the contract's document media type or an action CTA, never as an image, and hero/featured slots hold images; `artifactHandling.legacyFallbacksUsed` is false AND the surrounding notes show it is true by fact, not just by schema constant. A text-only candidate with `artifactReferences: []` and notes explaining that no media slots exist scores full marks — absence of media is not absence of rigor. Score 3: forms are correct but provenance is thin — a reference is pattern-valid with no verification evidence, and the output treats it as trusted rather than as untrusted metadata plus a blocker. Score 0 — any of: a raw artifact key sitting in a rendered field WITHOUT a corresponding entry in `blockers` (the contract says this breaks rendering, so it is a hard block; downgrading it to a `notes` warning is itself the 0); a remote URL, data URI, repo/src path, or hand-authored public path substituted for a protocol-materialized reference; a reference belonging to another request or slug; unverified media silently upgraded to trusted; a document rendered into an image slot; or `legacyFallbacksUsed: false` asserted while the notes/references show a fallback was in fact used.

criteria.name: Builds, does not publish — no client state mutated
criteria.description: Every client interaction evidenced in the output is read-only. The node must not have created, patched, checked out, published, released, or triggered a build on any client object, and must not claim to have done so.
criteria.guidance:
Judged from the output's own record of its interactions (`contractSource.primary`/`secondary`, `clientValidation`) plus the execution tool log where the judge is given it. Full marks (5): every recorded client interaction names `project.call_read_tool` with a read-only operation (object_contract, object_get, object_inventory, object_validate, registry_get, search); no create/patch/publish/release/checkin/checkout/build/retire/submit_review operation appears anywhere; where a write was genuinely required to proceed (e.g. no draft record exists to validate against), the output hands that off as a `blockers` entry for a downstream write-enabled step instead of performing it. Score 3: no write is evidenced, but the record is incomplete — interactions asserted without naming the tool/operation, so read-only status must be taken on trust. Score 0 — any of: a write-risk operation recorded or described as performed from this node; `project.call_tool` used for a read or for anything at all here; the summary/notes claiming an object was created, patched, submitted, published or released; or a draft id presented as if this node had obtained one by writing. Note that a payload can be perfect on every other criterion and still earn 0 here — mutating client state during assembly is the failure mode this node exists to make impossible.

REWEIGHTED + VETOED (Session B2 follow-up, 2026-08-03): weight lowered 2.25 -> 1.25 and criticalMin:0 added. Two separate problems, two separate fixes. (1) This criterion scores the model's own narration of its behavior, so a node that wrote silently and said nothing previously scored the SAME 5/5 as one that honestly recorded read-only calls — rewarding non-disclosure. Fix: when toolCalls evidence is supplied to the judge, score primarily from the recorded operations; when it is not supplied, score from narration but CAP at 3/5 regardless of how clean the narration reads — an unverified 'read-only' claim cannot earn full marks. (2) A proven write is the single worst thing this node can do — mutating client state during what is contractually a build — and must fail the whole rubric outright, which is why criticalMin:0 was added on top of the lower weight: a real write vetoes regardless of every other score.

criteria.name: Identifiers follow the contract's declared form and refer to the right things
criteria.description: clientProjectId, clientObjectType, requestId, slug and any object/draft id follow the client contract's declared conventions and point at the correct entities for THIS request; where a safe id cannot be derived, it is omitted with a stated reason rather than invented.
criteria.guidance: Full marks (5): `clientProjectId` and `clientObjectType` are non-empty and match the project and object type the contract was actually fetched for (contractSource arguments agree with clientObjectType); `slug` and any object id conform to the contract's stated pattern; `requestId`, when present, matches the client's declared request-id convention and belongs to the current run; when the convention cannot be satisfied safely, `requestId` is OMITTED and a `validationAssumptions` or `notes` entry states explicitly why (e.g. no client-confirmed sequence number available in a read-only node) — omission with a reason scores as well as a correct id. Score 3: identifiers are plausible and internally consistent but one is unexplained — e.g. requestId present with no stated derivation, or clientObjectType asserted while contractSource was fetched for a different type. Score 0 — any of: a hand-fabricated requestId or object id shaped to look conforming but not derived from the client (inventing an id to unblock a downstream step is the specific abuse here); an id borrowed from another request, run, or slug; clientProjectId/clientObjectType that contradict `contractSource`; or an id that violates the contract's stated pattern while the output claims conformance.

criteria.name: No workspace-only fields cross into the client payload
criteria.description: clientObject contains only fields the client's fetched contract declares. Internal workflow scaffolding must stay out of the object that a publisher would send.
criteria.guidance:
SEAM RULE (Wolf, 2026-08-03): the test is not a field-name blacklist. A field belongs in clientObject iff the client's contract declares it AND its content is publication-owned, not CMS-agent-owned. CMS-agent-owned content — general craft guidance, DTC/marketing technique, security notes, AI run limitations/operating conditions, workflow or pipeline commentary — must never appear inside clientObject, regardless of what field it sits in; that includes fields whose NAME sounds client-facing (e.g. publication_context) if their CONTENT is actually a CMS-agent operating note. Publication-owned content — this piece's subject, this client's rules, this object's structure — may cross only where the contract declares the field.

5: every field in clientObject is either contract-anchored (named in notes/validationAssumptions as contract-declared) or is plainly publication-specific content; no field's CONTENT is CMS-agent's own professional/process material; any workflow-side commentary lives in the payload's sibling fields (notes, validationAssumptions, blockers), never inside clientObject.
3: one field leaks into clientObject whose content is ambiguous between profession- and publication-owned, and the output does not flag which it judged it to be.
0 — any of: a field inside clientObject whose CONTENT is CMS-agent's own craft/process material (general writing advice, an AI run condition, a security caveat, workflow commentary) regardless of the field's name; an internal identifier or run metadata inside a reader-visible field; secrets, authorization headers, storage grants, scoped upload tokens or blob credentials anywhere in the output (automatic 0 regardless of placement); or an invented root field presented as contract-declared when it is not. The test is content, not name — 'is this field's actual content the client's business, or the CMS agent's own' — not a lookup against a fixed list of field names.

criteria.name: Contract provenance is recorded and governs the payload
criteria.description: contractSource shows the client's own contract was actually fetched for this object type, with enough detail to audit it, and that contract — not a workspace-local schema — governed the payload's shape.
criteria.guidance: Added because `contractSource` is a REQUIRED field of this node's output schema and 'missing or unprovenanced contract' is an explicit blocker condition in the node prompt; without it the other conformance criteria have nothing to conform to. Full marks (5): `contractSource` records status fetched, the tool and read-only operation used, the object_type fetched, a fetch timestamp, and the fingerprint (or an explicit note that the contract publishes none); secondary lookups that informed the payload (taxonomy, inventory, registry) are listed with what each established; `validationAssumptions` states that the fetched contract — not a workspace-local content schema — is the governing shape. Score 3: a contract was fetched and named but the record is thin (no timestamp, no operation, or no statement of what governed the shape), leaving the payload auditable only by inference. Score 0 — any of: `contractSource` empty, placeholder, or describing a workspace-local schema; a contract asserted as fetched with no tool/operation evidence; a stale or different-object-type contract used to justify the payload's shape; or the payload's fields visibly following a workspace content model while `contractSource` claims client governance.

metadata.proposedWeightRationale:
Highest weight goes to gates_preserved (3.0). This is the last structured step before the publish gates, and since the operator opened publishing globally on 2026-07-31 the payload's own honesty — dryRun literally true, the client's real validator verdict, blockers stated at full strength — is a real line of defense rather than a formality. A payload that flatters its readiness is the single most expensive failure this node can produce.

Second is body_fidelity (2.5): the whole point of the approval chain upstream is that what got approved is what ships; content authored or altered at the adapter step launders unapproved text past review. It is weighted below gates only because a fidelity slip is still catchable by a human reading the draft, whereas a weakened gate is caught by nobody.

artifact_form_and_provenance and no_side_effects sit equal at 2.25. Both are hard-block territory: a raw key in a rendered field breaks the client's rendering (the contract says so, so it is a blocker and never a warning), and a write from this node mutates client state during what is contractually a build. They are weighted just above the 0.15 line deliberately — see the threshold note below.

identifier_conformance, no_workspace_fields and contract_provenance sit at 1.5 each. Each is a genuine correctness requirement, but a wrong id, a leaked internal key, or a thin provenance record is diagnosable and fixable before publish without having harmed anything — unlike the four above.

passThreshold 0.85 is set so that a zero on any of the four heavily-weighted criteria fails the rubric on its own arithmetic: with weights summing to 14.5, a single zero on gates (3.0), fidelity (2.5), artifacts (2.25) or side-effects (2.25) drops the normalized score to 0.79 / 0.83 / 0.845 / 0.845 respectively — all below the bar even with perfect marks everywhere else. A zero on one of the three lighter criteria lands at ~0.90 and survives, which is the intended asymmetry: id conventions and provenance detail are correctable, gate integrity is not. 0.85 is also defensible for this node specifically because these are conformance criteria, not taste — a correctly assembled payload should score 5s routinely, so the threshold is demanding without being aspirational. If the operator wants the bar to also fail single lapses in ids, workspace-field leakage or provenance, raise the threshold to 0.90 rather than reweighting.
metadata.nodeReadNotes:
Read the live node record (prompt, output schema, allowedTools, effectiveTools, metadata.canonicalRules) and the most recent real output (artifact_publish_payload_1785414570132, run run_1785405350649_9u5mjz) before writing any criterion. Every criterion binds to a field that actually exists in the schema: artifact (const), summary, clientProjectId, clientObjectType, contractSource, dryRun (const true), clientObject, requestId, clientValidation, artifactProtocol, artifactReferences, artifactHandling.legacyFallbacksUsed (const false), validationAssumptions, blockers, notes.

What the live read changed in my approach, and what cannot be judged from the output alone:

1. body_fidelity is the weakest criterion under output-only judging. An exact diff needs the upstream article_body output in the judge's context. The criterion is written to use that diff when supplied and to fall back on proxies (traceability, no newly-authored prose, no sources/claims/CTA destinations absent upstream, declared omissions) otherwise — and it caps at 2 rather than 5 when the output gives the judge no traceable basis at all, so the fallback cannot be gamed by an output that simply says nothing. Recommendation to the operator: feed article_body's output to the judge alongside publish_payload's for this node.

2. no_side_effects is fundamentally a trace property, not an output property. From the output alone the judge can only check *evidence and claims* of writes — the tool names and read-only operations recorded in contractSource/clientValidation, and any narrative claim of having created or patched an object. A node that wrote silently and said nothing would pass on output alone. The guidance names the execution tool log as authoritative where the judge is given it. If the operator wants this criterion load-bearing at its 2.25 weight, the judge harness should pass the node's tool-call log; otherwise treat the score as a proxy. Note the node's effectiveTools grant project.call_tool (write, approval-gated) as *allowed*, so the prohibition here is prompt-level, not enforced by the tool layer — which is precisely why it needs a rubric criterion.

3. Two schema constants (dryRun: true, artifactHandling.legacyFallbacksUsed: false) are enforced by the schema itself, so scoring them alone would hand out free marks. I wrote both as honesty tests instead: dryRun is scored together with whether the readiness story around it is truthful, and legacyFallbacksUsed:false earns 0 when the notes or references show a fallback was in fact used despite the constant. That is the anti-gaming guard for this node.

4. The one criterion added beyond the six required is contract_provenance. Justification: contractSource is a REQUIRED field of the output schema, and 'missing or unprovenanced contract' is an explicit blocker condition in the node prompt. It is also logically prior to three of the required concerns — identifier conventions, the workspace-vs-client field boundary, and artifact path forms are all defined BY the fetched contract, so without provenance those criteria have no reference to be judged against. No listed concern was dropped, and none were merged.

5. Scoring note grounded in the real output: the most recent run is a text-only article with artifactReferences: []. The artifact criterion states explicitly that an empty reference set plus notes explaining the absence of media slots earns full marks, so the rubric does not penalize text-only runs or push the node toward inventing media to look thorough. Similarly, that run omits requestId with a stated reason — the identifier criterion scores a reasoned omission as highly as a correct id, because the alternative is exactly the fabrication we are trying to prevent.

rubrics.name: artifact_plan.v1 — Media Verification & Cost-Shortcut Integrity Rubric (DRAFT)
rubrics.description: Scores an artifact_plan.v1 output: whether every media slot marked verified is actually backed by current-request verification evidence, whether the request id was confirmed against the client's own convention before any write (a real production incident — an orphaned artifact — happened exactly this way), whether the node's zero-media cost shortcut is taken only when genuinely warranted, and whether capability/budget limits are honestly reported rather than silently worked around. This node had no rubric before this revision despite being 12.9% of measured spend — the fifth rubric closes that gap.

criteria.name: Verified media is actually verified, not pattern-matched
criteria.description: Every slot marked has_trusted_artifact carries real verification evidence — matching key, digest, content type, size and timestamp for the CURRENT request — in its verification field. A pattern-valid key is never proof.
criteria.guidance:
5: every has_trusted_artifact slot's verification field names the artifact service's own verification evidence (key, digest, content type, size, timestamp) and that evidence is scoped to THIS request; slots without such evidence are needs_generation or blocked, never has_trusted_artifact.
3: verification is present but thin — key and content type only, no digest or timestamp — leaving provenance asserted rather than shown.
0: any slot is marked has_trusted_artifact with no verification field, a verification field that is empty or generic, or verification evidence that belongs to another request or slug. A single instance is 0 regardless of how many other slots are clean — this is the exact failure that puts the wrong image on a live client page.
VETO: criticalMin 0 — a fabricated-verified claim is categorically unacceptable and fails the whole rubric, matching how the equivalent failure is treated in article_body's media_safety and publish_payload's artifact_form_and_provenance.

criteria.name: Request id confirmed against the client's own convention before any write
criteria.description: requestId is derived from the CLIENT's declared id convention (requestIdConvention) and confirmed acceptable to the client (requestIdConfirmedByClient) before any artifact is materialized under it. Grounded in a real incident: a permissive id accepted by the artifact generator but rejected by the client's own index produced an orphaned artifact the client could never list, reconcile, or delete.
criteria.guidance:
5: requestIdConvention names the client's actual convention (not a generic pattern); requestIdConfirmedByClient is true only where the output shows real evidence of a client-side check; any slot materialized (has_trusted_artifact) carries a requestId that passed that check; where confirmation could not be obtained, slots are blocked rather than materialized under an unconfirmed id.
3: a convention is named and an id derived, but confirmedByClient is asserted with no evidence of the check having actually happened.
0: any of — a slot is materialized (has_trusted_artifact) under a requestId that was never confirmed; requestIdConfirmedByClient is true with no supporting evidence anywhere in the output; or requestIdConvention is absent while slots are materialized anyway. This is the orphaned-artifact failure mode by name — an artifact the client's own index will reject is worse than no artifact.
VETO: criticalMin 0 — an unconfirmed id backing a materialized artifact is a real, documented production failure, not a style concern.

criteria.name: Only the client's declared protocol, for this request
criteria.description: Every artifact reference came from the client's declared artifact protocol, materialized for the current request. No repo paths, remote URLs, data URIs, hand-authored keys, direct-save fallbacks, or references copied from another request or slug.
criteria.guidance:
5: artifactProtocol names the client's own declared protocol; every reference in media_slots and artifactReferences is in the form that protocol produces, scoped to this request; no reference is a URL, data URI, filesystem/repo path, or hand-authored key.
3: forms are correct but one reference's request-scoping is unstated, leaving it unverifiable rather than provably wrong.
0: any forbidden form appears anywhere in media_slots or artifactReferences — a single instance is 0.

criteria.name: Blocks on denied capability, timeout, or over-budget — never invents a pointer
criteria.description: When a required capability is denied by project policy, approval times out, or media exceeds the client's budget under a blocking rule, the node names the specific condition in blockers[] / requiredArtifactCapabilities and marks the slot blocked, rather than inventing a pointer or silently proceeding.
criteria.guidance:
5: every denial, timeout, or budget block the output's own evidence implies is reflected in blockers[] with the specific missing capability or reason named; requiredArtifactCapabilities lists exact capability names, not vague descriptions; no slot is has_trusted_artifact or needs_generation where the node's own evidence shows a block condition applied.
3: a block condition is mentioned in notes[] but not reflected in blockers[] or the slot's own status.
0: a slot proceeds (has_trusted_artifact or needs_generation with a synthesized reference) despite the output's own evidence of a denied capability, timeout, or blocking budget condition; or blockers[] is empty while the summary describes an unresolved condition.

criteria.name: The cost shortcut fires only when genuinely warranted
criteria.description: The zero-media shortcut (empty media_slots, no tool calls) is taken ONLY when the input body genuinely declares no media needs, and is NOT skipped — burning tool calls to prove an absence — when it is. This is the direct cost/quality tension for this specific node: its own historical $1.95/386K-token blowout was caused by NOT taking this shortcut on a text-only article.
criteria.guidance:
5: either (a) the input body has no media slots or artifact references and media_slots is empty with minimal-to-zero tool-call evidence (when supplied to the judge), or (b) the input body does declare media needs and every one of them appears as a slot in media_slots — the shortcut correctly NOT taken.
3: shortcut behavior is directionally correct but the output gives no evidence either way (no tool-call log, no explicit statement of why the shortcut was or wasn't used).
0: either direction of failure — the body declares real media needs but media_slots is empty or incomplete (the shortcut wrongly taken to save cost, silently dropping a requirement — the exact regression a cost trial on THIS node must be checked against), OR the body is genuinely media-free but the output shows turns/tool calls spent attempting to verify an absence (the exact failure that produced the recorded blowout).

criteria.name: Media budget and format decisions follow the client's stated policy
criteria.description: Over-budget media is flagged or blocked per the client's own declared rule, never silently shipped oversize or silently downgraded without note.
criteria.guidance:
5: where an artifact would exceed the client's declared budget, the output either blocks it (if the client's policy blocks) or flags it explicitly (if the client's policy warns), and states which rule applied; no oversize asset is shipped silently.
3: a budget concern is mentioned but not tied to which client rule (block vs flag) it followed.
0: an over-budget asset is present with no flag or block, or the output silently re-encodes/downgrades without recording that it did.

metadata.proposedWeightRationale:
materialization_verification (3.0) is heaviest and carries a criticalMin veto: a fabricated-verified claim ships the wrong image to a live client page, the same severity class as article_body's media_safety and publish_payload's artifact_form_and_provenance, both of which treat this as an automatic 0. request_id_confirmed (2.5, also vetoed) is second because it is not hypothetical — the node's own version history records a real orphaned-artifact incident caused by exactly this gap, which is why the client-confirmation step exists in the prompt at all. zero_media_shortcut_used_correctly (2.5) is weighted equally with request id because it is the ONE criterion that is symmetric to cost pressure in both directions — it fails a cheap run that drops real media AND fails an expensive run that wastes turns proving an absence, which is exactly the property needed since this node is a live cost target. no_legacy_fallback (2.0) and honest_blocking (2.0) are real correctness requirements but neither is a documented production incident, so they sit below the vetoed pair. budget_and_capability_honesty (1.0) is lightest — it matters but is the most forgivable and least likely to differentiate two model configurations.

passThreshold 0.85 matches the other conformance-style rubrics (contract_intelligence, article_body, publish_payload) because this node's failures are mostly mechanical/binary, not judgment calls: with total weight 13.0, a 0 on materialization (3.0) scores 0.769, on request_id (2.5) scores 0.808, on the shortcut (2.5) scores 0.808, on either 2.0-weight criterion scores 0.846 — all fail, matching intent. The two lightest, no_legacy_fallback's sibling weight class and budget_and_capability_honesty (1.0), score 0.923 on a solo zero and survive, which is deliberate: a thin format-policy note is correctable and should not fail an otherwise-clean plan.

Read the live node record (prompt, output schema, allowedTools, modelConfig, 7 revisions) before writing any criterion. The node's own version history directly justified two criteria: v64/v65 record a real production incident ("the permissive requestId pattern was the direct cause of an orphaned artifact in live testing — pdf-tool accepted an id the client's index rejected") which is exactly what request_id_confirmed hunts; and v259 records the node's own $1.95/386K-token cost blowout on a text-only article, which is exactly what zero_media_shortcut_used_correctly hunts in both directions. CRITERIA THAT CANNOT BE FULLY JUDGED FROM THE OUTPUT ALONE: materialization_verification and request_id_confirmed both ultimately depend on whether the artifact service's own verification actually happened, which the judge cannot independently confirm from the output text — the guidance scores whether the EVIDENCE FIELDS are populated with request-scoped specifics versus generic placeholders, which is the same proxy article_body's media_safety and publish_payload's artifact_form_and_provenance already use for the equivalent problem. zero_media_shortcut_used_correctly is sharper when the judge is given the input body (to know whether media was genuinely needed) and tool-call evidence (to know whether turns were spent); without either, guidance falls back to scoring internal consistency and caps at 3 when the output gives no evidence either way.
